Do different questions receive different help on Stack Overflow?¶

Zi Hu · Keyue Li · Yihan Wang — SOSC314

Project repository · Notebook · Reproduce

1. Research question and motivation¶

Online communities allocate both attention and assistance, meaning a fast reply does not always resolve a user's request, and a slower answer might. Therefore, this study investigates whether help-seeking intentions and technical subjects are associated with the helpfulness and speed of the first answer, and whether these observed patterns remain stable when accounting for variations in question composition and measurement. Understanding this relationship matters because answer speed and quality are distinct outcomes, and testing their robustness ensures that conclusions about community dynamics are reliable rather than artifacts of the data. Ultimately, success is defined by achieving interpretable and reproducible comparisons, rather than building a classification model that merely maximizes group differences.

2. Data and outcomes¶

The Python Questions from Stack Overflow archive supplies Questions, Answers and Tags from 2008–2016. Our unit is a question paired with its first observed human answer, ordered by creation time then answer ID. We measure initial help, not the best eventual answer. Response delay is the difference between recorded creation times.

Three disjoint batches contain 5,000 questions. The fine-score sample is nested, not another 1,000 independent questions. Technical-topic learning uses a separate 20,000-question sample; the response-prediction benchmark uses 60,000.

3. Problem setup¶

Tasks, targets and inputs¶

Main study: measurement and group comparison. NMF and LDA perform unsupervised topic modeling on question text or extracted verb phrases. Their outputs define groups; a fixed, prompted Qwen annotator assigns overlapping intention labels from questions and ordinal helpfulness ratings from question–first-answer pairs. We compare ratings and recorded first-answer delay across groups. No supervised model is trained to predict helpfulness; these comparisons do not establish annotation accuracy.

Separate benchmark: supervised binary classification. Inputs are question text/tags or structural and posting-time features; the target is whether a reply is observed within 24 hours (1/0), not helpfulness. Logistic regression uses the temporal training/validation/test split in Section 7. This does not estimate causal group effects.

Assumptions and scope¶

The first observed human answer represents initial help, not the best eventual answer. Assessment from visible text is imperfect: historical edits, unread links and missing runtime context matter. Fine-score means treat ordinal steps as equally spaced, not calibrated utility. Answered-only comparisons cannot describe unanswered questions. Overlapping labels require question-level resampling; associations are not assumed causal.

4. Methods¶

Technical topics and request categories¶

Yihan applies TF–IDF and Non-negative Matrix Factorization (NMF) to 20,000 questions. NMF is chosen because its inspectable topic-word weights provide direct interpretability. To improve granularity, four of the eight broad topics are subdivided, producing thirteen technical categories. The analysis shows that code-retaining preprocessing yields a greater dominant-topic weight (0.601 versus 0.542) and fewer assignments below 0.5 (35.5% versus 46.3%). However, because HTML/URL handling also differs, this comparison does not isolate the effect of code removal alone.

Figure 1. Topic-method diagnostics. NMF concentration/ambiguity and Doc2Vec silhouette ranges assess different properties, not classification accuracy. K varies from 4 to 10 for the silhouette ranges.

The study also explored Doc2Vec followed by k-means as a conventional dense-document alternative to NMF's sparse TF–IDF inputs, not as a state-of-the-art encoder. This tests whether learned document embeddings yield better-separated clusters. The initial PV-DBOW model (100 dimensions, 20 epochs) and an alternative PV-DM model (200 dimensions, 50 epochs) both produced weak or negative silhouette scores, suggesting overlapping clusters under these tested settings rather than clear geometric separation. Weak separation and interpretable NMF terms motivated retaining NMF for exploration; they do not establish universal superiority or validate semantic topic assignments.

Figure 2. Yihan's supplied 13-category similarity heatmap. Cosine similarity between category mean TF–IDF vectors measures shared vocabulary. Related subdivisions can remain similar without being identical; the heatmap does not validate label accuracy.

Keyue follows Allamanis and Sutton's verb-phrase approach: up to three phrases per question, a 694-phrase vocabulary, ten archived LDA topics trained on 59,870 questions, then a mapping to five request categories.

Figure 3. Keyue's archived LDA topic display. Representative phrases make the mapping interpretable; ten latent topics are not the same as five final categories. Bars are model weights, not frequencies or accuracy.

Strict labels use archived text; recovered labels use current Stack Exchange API text with the same model, vocabulary, mapping and processing pipeline, as reported by Keyue. About 62% of recovered texts were edited after 2016. Before score filtering, her accounting is 3,423 strict + 1,568 recovered + four deleted + five without extractable verb phrases = 5,000.

Qwen as an annotator, not an answer generator¶

Qwen2.5-Coder-14B-Instruct evaluates existing human answers. Inspected runs use local float16 inference on remote NVIDIA L20 GPUs, greedy decoding and seed 314, without fine-tuning. Coding orientation and feasible repeated inference motivated selection; we did not establish best annotator accuracy. Server software differs and the upstream weight revision is unpinned.

Figure 4. Annotation workflow. Intent sees the question only; helpfulness sees the question and first answer. Outputs and manual inspections inform analysis without replacing frozen labels.

Intent decisions are yes/no/uncertain, with question-line evidence for positives. Coarse scoring returns relevance, actionability, sufficiency and a separate overall 0–2 judgment: unhelpful, partial or substantial. Overall is not their sum. Fine scoring uses 0–10 anchors and states request, help and remaining gap. Format uses structured-output clarification; Scope additionally emphasizes the expressed request rather than requiring an entire implementation. Shared anchors do not make this a pure scale-resolution experiment.

Inputs exceeding 7,500 tokens are skipped; output caps are 256 tokens for coarse/intent and 512 for fine. JSON/citation checks establish protocol compliance, not correctness. The model neither runs answer code nor reads linked pages. Full prompts and a recorded example are supplied.

5. Results: do groups receive different help?¶

The main coarse sample and fine-score sensitivity¶

Of 4,986 valid coarse ratings, 4,382 (87.9%) are substantial. Across LDA categories, substantial shares range from 85.4% for does-not-work to 89.0% for implement. Most observed first answers therefore receive high coarse ratings, leaving modest descriptive separation between categories.

Figure 5. LDA request categories and helpfulness. Left: all 4,977 valid classified coarse cases. Right: fine means on 991 pooled cases and 684 strict cases. Panels have different supports and are not a before/after scale experiment.

The high concentration in the top coarse category leaves variation within that category unobserved. A ceiling effect may therefore limit descriptive separation, but these comparisons do not isolate its contribution: fine-score rankings also depend on prompt wording and label provenance.

In pooled fine labels, does-not-work leads Format, while way-of-using leads Scope. On strict-only cases, way-of-using leads both. Classification provenance and prompting change apparent rankings; restricting labels also changes the sample, so this is not a causal recovery effect.

Figure 6. Seven intentions on identical support. Both panels use 989 questions; labels overlap, so category counts do not sum to 989. Right intervals are 4,000 whole-question bootstrap pointwise 95% intervals. Asterisks identify groups below 50.

Fine means differ descriptively, but no contrast excludes zero in simultaneous 95% bands across 21 intention pairs and two prompts. This limits strong category rankings; it does not demonstrate equivalence. Small API-change and learning groups remain particularly uncertain.

Technical context and question composition¶

Figure 7. Technical-topic means. Format and Scope use identical 993-question support with category-specific counts. Lines connect prompt means; they are not uncertainty intervals.

Library-oriented groups often score above API/server, but group sizes and question composition differ. Exploratory adjustment includes year, log question length and code presence.

Figure 8. Adjusting technical-topic contrasts. Differences in substantial-rating shares use 1,992 valid coarse cases, with API/server as reference and HC3 pointwise 95% intervals. These are observational comparisons.

The Python-basics/API gap shrinks from 8.21 to 4.40 percentage points; its adjusted interval is −1.10 to 9.90. No adjusted contrast excludes zero under the conservative 96-contrast rule. Attenuation is consistent with composition contributing to raw differences, not proof that topics have no association.

Code elements and first-answer helpfulness¶

Figure 9. Mean fine score by code-element count. The fixed 1,000-question sample yields 995 valid Format ratings and 996 valid Scope ratings, with each bar showing its bin-specific n. Each scoring arm uses all its valid ratings rather than being restricted to a strict common-support subset. Code elements count HTML <code> elements, including inline and block code, not code length. Black error bars indicate mean ±1 standard error (SE = s/√n, where s is the sample standard deviation), not 95% confidence intervals. Yihan supplied the figure and generation code; the bin means, counts, and standard errors were independently reproduced (bin statistics).

Mean ratings peak in the 3–5 element bin, with the Scope prompt averaging 7.31 compared to 6.06 for questions with no code elements. This pattern suggests that providing concrete code examples may help respondents better interpret a request. However, it does not establish an optimal amount of code or imply that longer code causes worse answers. Furthermore, code element count is not equivalent to code length, overall question composition varies, and the 11+ bin contains only 24 cases per prompt, limiting robust conclusions for that group.

Speed is a separate outcome¶

Figure 10. First-response speed. Group medians and differences use 1,987 intention-complete answered questions. Whole-question bootstrap preserves overlapping memberships. API usage is the reference; blue bands are pointwise and gray bands simultaneous 95%.

API-change's median is 60.26 minutes versus 24.41 for API usage. The 35.85-minute gap has a pointwise interval of −4.16 to 60.03. Additional context or specialized knowledge could delay replies, but these observations neither establish that mechanism nor imply all API questions receive slower answers.

Measurement sensitivity¶

Figure 11. Coarse/fine correspondence. On 993 identical pairs, dots show fine means and lines show interquartile ranges, not confidence intervals. Coarse groups contain 21, 100 and 872 cases.

Higher coarse categories have higher fine means, but substantial ratings span fine scores; no fixed conversion follows. Scope exceeds Format by 0.407 points on average (paired-bootstrap 95% interval 0.262–0.545): 277 increases, 126 decreases and 590 ties. Prompt effects are clearer than reliable intention rankings. Greater score dispersion alone does not establish a better measure.

6. Diagnostics and substantive interpretation¶

The authors manually inspected many questions, answers and ratings, without a uniform adjudication standard or recorded accuracy estimate. A separate GPT-assisted review covers 48 score-change-stratified cases, not a population error sample. In question 19851005, a local index-name change addresses the request, yet identical explanations accompany scores 10 and 9. In 21352016, the audit flags an input-representation mismatch and an unmet array-output request that both model explanations overlook. Runtime behavior and historical edits remain uncertain.

Yihan reports checking 15 questions per selected type. We reproduced all 28 supplied regex-feature percentages over the complete category groups in the separate 20,000-question corpus, not merely those review cases.

The textual feature comparison reveals distinct structural differences. Web-development questions show markedly higher usage of request/response terminology (39.0% for API/Server and 31.7% for Django vs. ~1% for NumPy/Matplotlib) and authentication-related terms (17.4% and 20.9% vs. under 1%). Error mentions are also more frequent in web categories (30.5% and 32.0% vs. 20.5% and 16.6%). This indicates that data-science questions are generally more localized, while web questions involve more multi-component interactions and external configuration.

Why Data Science Questions May Be Easier to Answer

NumPy and Matplotlib questions are typically localized and well-defined, asking for a specific transformation or formatting adjustment. For example, tasks might involve converting a list to a 2D array (ID: 6047243) or changing specific axis label colors (ID: 21240195). These clear inputs and recognizable goals often follow reusable programming patterns, allowing the model to easily map the question to a familiar template without needing broad system context.

Why Web Development Questions May Be Harder to Answer

In contrast, API/Server and Django questions are harder to answer because they involve multi-component interactions, such as connecting a client, proxy, and server simultaneously (ID: 39948448). They also depend heavily on external configuration and version-specific behaviors, as seen when adding TLS to a local app (ID: 40044040). Furthermore, there is often no single correct solution, as the best approach may depend on design preferences, such as choosing between overriding a save() method or using signals (ID: 6296584). These complexities make them much harder to diagnose from text alone than localized NumPy or Matplotlib tasks.

Allamanis and Sutton (2013) distinguish technical subjects from information sought. Beyer et al. (2020) compare automated seven-category classification. Our LDA adaptation and overlapping Qwen labels connect those distinctions to help and speed; they do not reproduce the papers' supervised accuracy. Our substantive extension is that observed rankings depend on annotation and text provenance, not solely category definitions.

7. Separate benchmark: predicting a reply within 24 hours¶

Structured logistic regression uses lengths, tag/code/link/question-mark counts and posting time; numeric features are standardized and time categories one-hot encoded. Text models use title, natural-language body and tags: TF–IDF word/word-pair features or frozen MiniLM embeddings, followed by class-balanced logistic regression. Encoders are not fine-tuned. A temporal split trains through 2014 (33,896), validates on 2015 (13,366) and tests on 2016 (12,738). ROC-AUC measures ranking; average precision must be read against 69.84% positive prevalence.

Table 3. Reply prediction on the 2016 test set

Text improves ranking relative to the structured baseline. This benchmark predicts reply availability, not helpfulness or why replies arrive. The table reproduces saved original-run metrics, not refitted models. Answer-derived predictors are excluded, but later question edits may leak posting-time-unavailable information.

8. Takeaways, limitations and future work¶

While category groupings reveal useful descriptive patterns, adjusting for question characteristics weakens some observed gaps, and differences in scoring prompts alter the final rankings. Since speed, usable assistance, and complete request coverage are distinct metrics, these findings caution against treating technical categories as a stable ranking of answer quality.

The study has several limitations. First, the reliance on historical Python data, answered-only selection, historical text edits, and small group sizes limits generalization. Second, the authors conducted many manual checks, but these did not use a uniform adjudication procedure or yield a formal estimate of annotation accuracy. Shared annotation-model biases could therefore create or conceal associations. Third, the feature analysis and examples are descriptive and cannot establish causal mechanisms. Future work should establish shared rules for manual checks, explicitly document model and text versions, define observation windows for unanswered questions, and conduct a conditional second-answer analysis restricted to insufficient first responses.
